newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-ITALIANS POISED TO STEAL THE SHOW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-ITALIANS POISED TO STEAL THE SHOW.

text.p: The F.A. Cup final, that quintissentially English soccer celebration with its hymn singing, marching bands and Royal patronage, will enjoy a distinctly Latin flavour this season.
The first goal for either Chelsea or Middlesbrough will like as not be scored by an Italian, from an Italian pass or a Brazilian free kick and from a move started by a Frenchman or Romanian.

Middlesbrough's silver-haired striker Fabrizio Ravanelli, with 31 goals this season, and Chelsea's diminutive magician Gianfranco Zola, who has enchanted the premier league with his consummate skill, will compete for centre stage at Wembley.
Further back Chelsea's Roberto Di Matteo patrols the midfield with calm assurance, while Middlesbrough's Gianluca Festa can crush an opponent's attacking venture soon as look at it.

Then there is Italy's former international Gianluca Vialli, who alongside Ravanelli led Juventus to the European cup this time last year, but is now desperate to get off the bench and prove to Chelsea he is not past it.

Only talent-laden Brazilian Juninho, who worked so hard for Middlesbrough in their vain attempt to avoid relegation can steal the limelight from the Italians, who have taken the English league by storm.
Despite their popularity they have not all had an easy ride this season.
Ravanelli, in particular, has found the experience of living in England's industrial north east and fighting relegation instead of chasing glory with Juventus alien and disturbing.
"It's not a happy time for me," he said earlier this season. "Fabrizio Ravanelli needs to win."

The 28-year-old joined Middlesbrough in the close season for seven million pounds sterling ($11.5 million), lured, he said, by the prospect of working for manager Bryan Robson, whom he had admired as an England international and by the challenge of winning honours at a club which has failed to bring home a top trophy in its 122-year history.
He marked his debut with a hat-trick against Liverpool in the opening game of the season and has scored consistently since.
But he has slammed English football for its style and training methods.
"Here there is a different culture and a different mentality...the training methods are not adequate," he said as the club plummeted to the relegation zone at the end of last year.
"English players have a natural gift for running, but as for explosiveness and reaction time they can't match the Italians. In soccer you have to do more than run."

Despite revelling in his talent and enjoying his customary goal-scoring celebration of pulling his shirt over his face, fans and team mates have been hurt by Ravanelli's remarks and apparent disloyalty.
They were upset when he chose to return to Italy for treatment for a back injury last week instead of showing solidarity during the crucial final days of the championship.

Festa, who joined Middlesbrough from Internazionale the same January week that the club were docked three points by the F.A. for failing to turn to a fixture at Blackburn, has proved rather more discreet in his dealings with the club.
But the 28-year-old $4.4 million defender is unlikely to hang around with a club condemned to the lower divisions next season, unless they can beat Chelsea and win a place in the Cup Winners' Cup.
Vialli has made no secret of his disappointment and anger at being left on the bench in favour of the striking partnership of Zola and Welsh international Mark Hughes.

But he has been less vociferous in recent weeks after settling in a flat in the wealthy Belgravia district of London following months of searching for a suitable pied a terre, and after reaching an apparent understanding with Chelsea's player manager Ruud Gullit.
"If (players) want to go then I won't stop them. I don't want players here who aren't happy but I have a feeling they want to stay," Gullit said last week.
The former Dutch international, no stranger to top honours and Italian football himself, believes a spell in England has done his Italians good.
"Di Matteo was a holding player with Lazio. He's coming forward now much more. It's no coincidence he has just scored his first goal for Italy," Gullit said.

Both Di Matteo and Zola are obviously enjoying life close to London's trendy Kings Road, where there is no lack of necessities such as good Italian food and stylish clothes shops. Zola's children attend an English school.
"Because life is good on and off the pitch, it helps...I am playing the best football of my career, consistent every game,"
Zola arrived with the season well underway last November. "I had to settle myself very quickly," he said. "The Chelsea players helped me to be confident and the atmosphere is so good."

Dubbed "happy feet" by captain Dennis Wise, Zola's skill on the ball has endeared him to fans and earned him the admiration of opponents. Alex Ferguson, manager of league champions Manchester United and a man of few compliments, said he had not realised Zola was so gifted.
The Italian pipped Juninho for the honour of Footballer of the Year, voted by their peers.

Chelsea's homegrown players say the Italians' influence has been very positive. Both Wise and the club's longest serving campaigner Steve Clarke say their touch and control have improved because they they don't want to look less skilful than the imports and are trying harder.

One cultural difference the Italians are beginning to come to terms with is the English obsession with the F.A. Cup. No other national Cup is so keenly contested and the players have been bemused by their team mates' excitement.
The reception they all get when they step out on to the Wembley turf on Saturday will give them an indication. With their experience of the big stage, they are sure to rise to the occasion.
